channel.title: The Dig — NISQ algorithms
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the NISQ algorithms preset. Today’s ranked list centers on HPC-integrated quantum control and decoding, led by 2611.17652 as the main read for its FPGA real-time layer, NVQLink transport, and qLDPC decoder, with 2611.16285 and 2611.16271 as adjacent skims on multi-GPU decoder orchestration and hierarchical real-time QEC decoding, while 2611.16971 and 2611.18378 offer lower-relevance but potentially adaptable methods for low-cost error mitigation and variational-circuit trainability screening. No pay dirt today — 1 to skim.

item.title: Structure makes quantum circuits trainable
item.description:
Skim theory — Gradients avoid barren plateaus if ρ⊗2 and ℳ⊗2 concentrate on the same irreducible invariant subspace of polynomial dimension moved inverse-polynomially by the differentiated gate. For an SU(n) ansatz with non-algebra observable X(1)X(2), variance decays as 2/n2, matching the exact formula (2n3−3n−2)/(n2(n−1)(n+1)2).

Grade 0.382 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes” · Wenbo Xie, Wojciech Szpankowski, Ananth Grama

Figure

Gradient variance versus number of qubits n from 4 to 20. Solid line shows the exact analytical variance (2n3−3n−2)/(n2(n−1)(n+1)2) decaying as 2/n2, compared against the analytical lower bound and circuit run estimates.

Asks

Does a given parameterized quantum circuit necessarily induce a barren plateau for arbitrary states and observables?

Before

Lie-algebraic frameworks assume the observable is generated by the circuit's Lie algebra 𝔤; for X(1)X(2) under number-conserving fermionic circuits, this accounted for only 56% of gradient variance at n=4 and 50% asymptotically.

But

Bounds are generally not tight. Requires circuit segments on both sides of the differentiated gate to form 2-designs for exact variance; sampling relative precision requires exponential runs if variance is exponentially small.

Tools

tensor-square representation decomposition · compact Lie groups · Schur orthogonality · variance sampling algorithm · parameter-shift rule

Abstract

The scalability of variational quantum algorithms is limited by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially in system size. This worst-case result raises fundamental questions about the trainability of quantum AI models. We present a major advance towards resolving this trainability question by answering whether a given quantum circuit has a barren plateau. We do this using an analytical framework that bounds the gradient variance for arbitrary input states ρ and observables M by decomposing the unitary representation of the associated compact Lie group. When the circuit segments on both sides of a gate form 2-designs, we obtain the variance exactly and prove a sufficient condition for trainability: if ρ^(⊗2) and M^(⊗2) are sufficiently concentrated on the same irreducible invariant subspace of polynomial dimension, and the differentiated gate moves this subspace by an inverse-polynomial amount, then the gradient variance is at least inverse-polynomial. We further present a sampling algorithm that estimates the gradient variance from runs of the ansatz, without constructing the representation-theoretic projectors. Our algorithm decides whether the variance exceeds a tolerance τ with the number of runs polynomial in 1/τ, including cases in which the bounds are inconclusive. This resolves the question of the trainability of the circuit before expensive training procedures.

arxave:action.title: Screen VQA ansätze for Annex8_2 benchmarks

item.arxave:action: Prototype the paper's gradient-variance estimator on small spin-qubit QAOA/VQE MaxCut circuits to see whether it can flag untrainable ansätze before running the Annex8_2 application benchmark.

arxave:action.title: Check assumptions for noisy 16-qubit spin-qubit hardware

item.arxave:action: Ask the authors whether the 2-design and polynomial-run guarantees survive limited connectivity, gate noise, and readout error typical of a 16-qubit spin-qubit device.
